articles.title: If You See Orange Flames on Your Gas Stove, This Is What It Means
articles.content:
Cooks have long loved the distinctive whoosh of firing up a gas stove. The flames pop up quickly and provide consistent heat, making it easy to cook with pinpoint control. Gas stoves also save the day if you need to cook when the power’s out because they don’t require electricity (for the cooking part, anyway). As a cook and an electrician, I wouldn’t give up mine for anything.
Unfortunately, gas stoves hide lurking dangers behind that satisfying flame. One major problem is air quality. We’ll dig into the specifics below, but in a recent study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, researchers found that nearly 13% of childhood asthma in the United States is caused directly by gas stoves. And that’s just one of the findings.
Even a perfectly functioning gas stove gives off invisible fumes. But keeping your eyes peeled for odd flame colors can help you diagnose major safety risks before they get out of hand. To find out more about gas stoves and safety, I spoke to Troy Legg, a virtual appliance technician with home-warranty company American Home Shield. He has more than 20 years of experience repairing appliances, including gas stoves, and knows exactly what color the flames should be.
Read on to find out what it means if you see different colors and what you should be doing to keep your gas stove in tip-top shape.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more safety, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
“A healthy gas-burner flame is usually blue,” Legg says. There’s room for a tiny bit of variation, but not much. “With natural gas, a blue flame with a slight white tip can be normal,” Legg adds. “With liquid propane, a blue flame with a small yellow tip can also be normal.”
But if most of the flame, not just the tip, turns a different color, that’s a signal that something is wrong.
Blue flames indicate that complete combustion of natural gas is taking place. Natural gas is mostly methane, and when it burns correctly on your stove, all of the fuel gets used up and turned into heat, water vapor and carbon dioxide (CO2). The flames are blue because the light produced within this clean-burning flame has a short wavelength. (Remember the ROYGBIV of a rainbow? The red side has longer wavelengths, and the blue-indigo-violet side has shorter ones.)
Natural gas produces a very hot flame—as high as 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit. In contrast, wood fires burn cooler and less cleanly, giving off soot and wood particles. It’s these particles that produce the campfire-like orange and red flames you should never see on your gas cooktop.
“A steady yellow or orange flame can signal incomplete combustion, often caused by dirty burners, blocked openings or an improper gas-to-air mixture,” Legg says. Instead of methane converting to CO2 and water vapor, some of the gas is not used and is released into the air, which is not ideal.
But not all situations are reason to panic. “A small amount of white or yellow tipping can be normal depending on the type of gas and the appliance,” Legg says. Dust in the air can create brief yellow flickers, and he says calcium and other minerals may burn orange. “But a flame that is mostly yellow, orange or red should be checked by a professional.”
Because blue flames are the normal state of affairs, the sudden appearance of orange or yellow means your stove is trying to tell you something. Here’s why these flames can be a big problem.
“A steady yellow or orange flame may mean the burner is dirty or the gas and air are not mixing properly,” Legg says. Either one can “affect combustion and potentially create a carbon monoxide (CO) risk,” he says. According to the EPA, the air around a properly working gas stove contains about 5 to 15 parts per million (ppm) of CO, and a poorly adjusted one can have levels of 30 ppm or higher.
Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that kills hundreds of people every year and sends 100,000 to the emergency room, according to the CDC. Children are particularly vulnerable, as are the elderly and people with breathing conditions. If you have a gas stove, putting in a CO monitor to alert you of high CO levels can be a lifesaver.
Orange flames are inefficient and will cost you money. In incomplete combustion, some of the gas coming out of your burners is flat-out wasted, so you have to use more gas to get the right amount of heat for cooking. That will translate into a higher gas bill over time.
Besides dangerous CO buildup, gas stoves are also known to contribute to poor indoor-air quality more generally (remember that asthma stat). Methane, nitrogen dioxide, benzene and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are released from even well-functioning stoves, and if your stove burns inefficiently, it gives off more of them.
This one’s not dangerous, but it could be disappointing if you’re hungry. Gas flames that are uneven or inefficiently burning, which often happens when you’re seeing those orange or yellow flames, can create hot spots, make you crank up the heat and otherwise decrease the quality of your cooking experience.
Legg says the main one to watch out for is red. “A red flame is less common and could point to an issue with gas quality, so homeowners should contact their gas provider if they see a persistent red flame,” he says. Gas-quality problems can include a range of issues, from an inconsistent delivery pressure to the presence of impurities that affect how the gas burns.
Another interesting twist involves the presence of a humidifier in your home. Humidifiers give off water vapor, of course, but that vapor also carries minerals like calcium and potassium. Legg mentioned calcium’s orange color earlier, but also be on the lookout for potassium’s pink or purple hue. Though these color changes are not dangerous, using distilled water will reduce these effects.
“Start with basic cleaning and inspection,” Legg says. “Make sure the burner cap is seated correctly, then check the burner openings for food, grease or debris.” Turn all knobs to the off position and remove the burner caps and heads. “A paper clip can be used gently to clear blocked burner holes and the small center orifice,” Legg says. Don’t use a wooden toothpick—it might break off, which could block the port and cause gas to back up.
You can also wash the parts of the burner assembly, but avoid soaking them. “Use a damp cloth instead of a soapy or wet cloth, since excess moisture can get into the spark switches and cause unwanted sparking,” Legg says. “After cleaning, make sure all parts are completely dry and properly reassembled before trying the burner again.”
“If the flame remains yellow, orange or red, or if there is any gas smell, stop using the appliance and contact a qualified repair technician or the gas provider,” Legg says. “An unusual flame color or smell can indicate a serious matter and potential safety risk. So if you notice something questionable, don’t wait to contact a professional or your gas provider.”

articles.title: Teens Are Getting Arrested After Posting a Dr. Seuss Meme—Here’s What’s Going On
articles.content:
At the risk of sounding old, it’s hard to keep up with what kids are doing online these days. Even uttering that sentence puts me firmly in the relic category, but … 6-7? Come on now! What are we even doing here?
The latest viral meme, involving a Dr. Seuss character who is definitely not teaching the youth their ABCs, seems silly and ridiculous at first glance—but is actually pretty terrifying. Sharing the meme has also had some very real, very scary consequences that you and your kids should be aware of.
I’ve been on the internet since the mid-1990s, so I have some big Gen X energy around online trends. My biggest fear was getting caught illegally downloading a few songs from Napster. (Which I barely did! I love copyright law!) But when I got a look at this creepy new meme, it had me wishing for the good old days.
To find out about this internet trend that’s increasingly getting the police called and has even led to some teen arrests, I spoke with Lt. Steven Orcutt with the Potter County Sheriff’s Department in Texas. Read on to learn what this viral trend is, why it’s a big deal and how to protect your children from consequences that could follow them around for life.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, cleaning, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
@cnn Videos showing a person dressed up as Cat in the Hat roaming streets after dark have spread across social media, even prompting responses from police in Ireland and the UK. But it remains unclear which, if any, of the sightings are real or if they are AI-generated. #catinthehat ♬ original sound – CNN
It’s called the Cat in the Hat meme. “This current trend began as a dark-humor meme using clips from the 2003 Cat in the Hat movie,” says Orcutt. “It has since evolved into an AI-generated hoax trend, where users create realistic-looking images and videos of the Cat in the Hat lurking around homes, neighborhoods, schools and other public spaces.”
The posts started on Snapchat and were circulating in Ireland and the U.K. in August, according to the Guardian. From there, they made their way across the ocean and to multiple platforms, including TikTok and, to a lesser degree, Instagram. The posts can be accompanied by creepy music and even threatening messages.
“Many posts claim the character is ‘coming to’ a specific town, school or community in a way of inciting fear or making vague statements of harm,” Orcutt says. Case in point: “On my way to Kentucky next, be looking out,” read one Cat in the Hat message on TikTok. Sometimes the meme has a real-life element, and the character is filmed chasing actual people.
But no matter what form the meme takes, the idea is to sow fear and confusion. “While the trend is not tied to real-world violence, it creates several issues,” Orcutt says.
“In short, it’s an internet hoax,” Orcutt says, “but the reaction to it can create real-world problems.”
Yes, several. “This is a national social media hoax, and not a localized threat,” Orcutt says. Teens from all over the country have been caught up in the hype and aftermath.
A 14-year-old in Grand Junction, Colorado, was arrested after posting a version of the meme that referenced a threat to a middle school. A 15-year-old Kansas kid was also detained over the meme, and in Oxford, Mississippi, a “juvenile” is facing terrorism-related charges over threats made to a “large school,” according to Mississippi’s WTVA.
Kids in Louisiana, Connecticut, Georgia and Texas have also been detained. “The Potter County Sheriff’s Office has processed one juvenile in relation to the investigation in our jurisdiction,” Orcutt says. “We, as an agency, encourage those who view anything of this nature to report it when seen and allow us the opportunity to properly investigate for any potential threats.”
For now, it’s continuing to rise—or at least, reports are on the rise. “These trends will continue to be shared, when seen, until the next wave of trends hit,” Orcutt says. In other words, until the next Socrates-and-skeletons viral meme surfaces, we’re stuck with creepy images of a life-sized human-cat hybrid.
“Although there is no real threat, the imagery can be unsettling, especially for younger students, and posts sometimes spread quickly enough to prompt public worry,” he adds. Be aware, too, that media reports have a tendency to elevate trends to larger-than-life proportions.
That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t take them seriously, but it’s important to keep the threats in perspective. “Locally, reported concerns seem to have been minimal and largely centered around students asking if the images and locations depicted are real,” Orcutt says.
“Parents can play a huge role in reducing the fear and preventing any potential escalation by simply talking openly with their children about hoax trends, reassuring kids that these videos are fabricated and not real, [and] asking their children to report any alarming posts to the proper authorities,” Orcutt says.
Also, parents should explain the potential legal consequences of sharing hoax threats involving schools and students, and “most importantly, be involved with their children by monitoring their social media usage,” he adds.
The post Teens Are Getting Arrested After Posting a Dr. Seuss Meme—Here’s What’s Going On appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Cereal in Each State—Did Your Breakfast Favorite Make the List?
articles.content:
Labor Day weekend is over, and summer is in the rearview mirror for another year. You know what that means: school. And as you rush your kids out the door to the bus or carpool, it’s likely with a bowl of cereal in their bellies.
My mom didn’t let us have “sugar cereals,” as she called them, so whenever I got the chance (at a friend’s house, usually), I’d devour Peanut Butter Cap’n Crunch like I’d been starving in the desert for weeks. Then it was back to Cheerios—though I’ve moved on to cereals with even less sugar these days. Getting old is fun!
As cereal season gets underway for another year, we thought it would be fun to take a look at which cereals are the most popular around the country. And lucky for us, CSP Global, which offers accredited nursing programs in St. Paul, Minnesota, and Portland, Oregon, had already done the heavy lifting.
Ahead, I’ll take you state by state through their delicious survey results filled with cereals you remember as a kid and eat now as an adult. Read on to get a bowlful of knowledge about this breakfast favorite.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food news, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
We do a lot of Googling these days, so instead of mining grocery stores for sales data or calling people on their phones (who answers those calls, anyway?), CSP Global analyzed Google Trends data to find out exactly which cereals Americans were hungry for.
Why did they do this, you might ask? Because they’re a nursing school, CSP Global wanted to get a sense of state and regional trends to start a conversation about nutrition and health. Cereal aisles across the country look pretty much the same, but when you really drill down on what people are searching for, some definite trends emerge.
When you take a look at this list, it’s apparent there’s not a lot of turnover in the cereal world. These are the same old classics we’ve been eating for decades. My mother would definitely not approve of most of them, but they sure sound delicious to me right about now.
Here are the most popular cereals in each state:
Froot Loops took the cereal crown with wins in 13 states and was by far the most searched cereal in the entire country. And it wasn’t even close: The tropical-fruit-flavored sugar bomb’s closest competition, Cheerios (yes!) and Rice Krispies, each won only 5 states apiece.
The cereal analysts also broke out the searches regionally, and it looks like the South gave Froot Loops its dominating win. The Northeast and the Midwest (my old stomping ground) went for the basic grains. Out in the sunny West, Honey Bunches of Oats came in first.
My beloved old home state of Minnesota was the only state to pick Wheaties … which actually isn’t too much of a surprise, now that I think of it. A Minneapolis radio station aired the very first cereal jingle in 1926, and it was for, yep, Wheaties.
What is surprising is that wheat, in general, turns out to be an unpopular cereal grain, at least as far as searches go. Raisin Bran won only one state, Maine, and Frosted Mini-Wheats also came out on top in a single state, Wyoming.
Here’s another head-scratcher: When is the last time you ate Apple Jacks? I didn’t even know it was still around, but Mississippi loves it. Finally, my old neighbor Iowa is the only state pulling for Cap’n Crunch (but not the clearly superior Peanut Butter version). Funny, I would have thought they’d be all-in for Corn Pops.

  • Georgia: Froot Loops

  • Idaho: Rice Krispies
  • Illinois: Cookie Crisp
  • Indiana: Golden Crisp
  • Iowa: Cap’n Crunch
  • Kansas: Trix
  • Kentucky: Froot Loops
  • Louisiana: Froot Loops
  • Maine: Raisin Bran
  • Maryland: Cinnamon Toast Crunch
  • Massachusetts: Trix
  • Michigan: Froot Loops
  • Minnesota: Wheaties
  • Mississippi: Apple Jacks
  • Missouri: Froot Loops
  • Montana: Rice Krispies
  • Nebraska: Lucky Charms
  • Nevada: Cocoa Pebbles
  • New Hampshire: Cheerios
  • New Jersey: Cookie Crisp
  • New Mexico: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • New York: Cheerios
  • North Carolina: Froot Loops
  • North Dakota: Special K
  • Ohio: Golden Crisp

  • Pennsylvania: Cheerios
  • Rhode Island: Fruity Pebbles
  • South Carolina: Cinnamon Toast Crunch
  • South Dakota: Rice Krispies
  • Tennessee: Cookie Crisp
  • Texas: Froot Loops
  • Utah: Rice Krispies
  • Vermont: Cheerios
  • Virginia: Froot Loops
  • Washington: Trix
  • Washington, D.C.: Trix
  • West Virginia: Corn Flakes
  • Wisconsin: Rice Krispies
  • Wyoming: Frosted Mini-Wheats

Which cereal earned the No. 1 spot in the most states?

Froot Loops took the cereal crown with wins in 13 states and was by far the most searched cereal in the entire country. And it wasn’t even close: The tropical-fruit-flavored sugar bomb’s closest competition, Cheerios (yes!) and Rice Krispies, each won only 5 states apiece.

What regional trends emerged?

The cereal analysts also broke out the searches regionally, and it looks like the South gave Froot Loops its dominating win. The Northeast and the Midwest (my old stomping ground) went for the basic grains. Out in the sunny West, Honey Bunches of Oats came in first.

  • Northeast: Cheerios
  • South: Froot Loops
  • West: Honey Bunches of Oats
  • Midwest: Rice Krispies

Were there any big surprises?

My beloved old home state of Minnesota was the only state to pick Wheaties … which actually isn’t too much of a surprise, now that I think of it. A Minneapolis radio station aired the very first cereal jingle in 1926, and it was for, yep, Wheaties.

What is surprising is that wheat, in general, turns out to be an unpopular cereal grain, at least as far as searches go. Raisin Bran won only one state, Maine, and Frosted Mini-Wheats also came out on top in a single state, Wyoming.

Here’s another head-scratcher: When is the last time you ate Apple Jacks? I didn’t even know it was still around, but Mississippi loves it. Finally, my old neighbor Iowa is the only state pulling for Cap’n Crunch (but not the clearly superior Peanut Butter version). Funny, I would have thought they’d be all-in for Corn Pops.

Sources:

  • CSP Global: “Every State’s Favorite Cereal”
  • University of Maryland: “Have you tried Wheaties? The Lost Art of Jingle Writing”

articles.title: It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy
articles.content:
二十五年转瞬即逝。2001年9月11日，四架飞机被劫持并直指美国心脏，自此生活一去不复返。尽管时间可能会淡化记忆，将它们推至内心的安全角落或延长回忆间隔，但那些可怕的视觉画面和亲身经历永远无法消弭。

令人难以置信的是，如今美国有三分之一的人是911事件之后出生的。然而，这场袭击的影响——增强的监控体制、加强的机场安全以及全球范围内的军事行动——深刻影响着每一个人。同样普遍的是那些关于英勇、友谊和牺牲的故事，它们将永远标记着那一天的悲伤。

随着911事件25周年的到来，我们整理了一份包含一些最重要新闻报道的清单，这些报道带我们回顾了事件发生当天的情况或从时间的角度重新审视。以下是关于2001年9月11日10篇引人注目的故事。其中一些已经被称颂了数十年；另一些你可能从未读过。

继续阅读，回顾这场悲剧，或许能在某些故事中找到希望。

2001年9月12日，美联社发表了一张一名男子从北塔头朝下坠落的照片。2003年，《绅士》杂志记者Tom Junod通过审查美联社摄影师Richard Drew拍摄的整套12张照片，试图确定这个人的身份。结果探讨了集体悲伤和创伤，并成为后911时代最具代表性的新闻报道之一。

[阅读更多](https://www.esquire.com/news-politics/a34755793/falling-man-911/)

标题中的“102分钟”指的是第一架飞机在8点46分撞击北塔和塔楼在10点28分坍塌之间的时间间隔。911事件发生八个月后，《纽约时报》通过拼凑被困者和遇难者的电子邮件和电话记录，以及幸存者的回忆，详细记录了那102分钟。时至今日，它依然令人毛骨悚然。

[阅读更多](https://www.nytimes.com/2002/02/24/nyregion/102-minutes.html)

《华尔街日报》的工作人员在2002年因对911事件的报道获得了普利策即时新闻报道奖。该报道包括对飞机和坍塌事件的实时报告，以及对机场安全和经济可能影响的分析。其中一个特别惊心动魄的故事是John Bussey撰写的第一人称叙事《风暴之眼：穿越绝望与混乱的旅程》。

[阅读更多](https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/wall-street-journal-staff)

这篇叙事作品于911事件后几日发表，将世贸中心、五角大楼以及联合航空93号航班在宾夕法尼亚州坠毁的最后时刻的事件编织在一起。David Maraniss通过幸存者的叙述和报道，重建了那一天的混乱和毁灭景象，并展示了亲历者当时的所见所感。

[阅读更多](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/2001-09-14/9-11-the-last-moments/)

Jennifer Senior对一个家庭在袭击后遭遇的悲剧的描述获得了2022年普利策特写报道奖。Bobby McIlvaine在2001年9月11日才26岁，这个关于他家人以不同方式面对失去他——一位魅力十足且雄心勃勃的儿子、兄弟和男友——的故事提醒我们，悲伤是无法预测且个人化的。

[阅读更多](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2021/08/bobby-mcilvaine-september-11-attack/619537/)

Rick Resorla是一位英国退役伞兵和美国陆军退役军人，担任摩根大通南塔的安全负责人。他因救出数千人而受到赞誉，却在回去提供帮助时遇难。James B. Stewart的这篇文章通过Resorla袭击前的个人生活以及其亲人的视角，讲述了那一天的故事。

[阅读更多](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2016/08/22/the-hero-of-the-world-trade-center)

这篇文章发表于911事件后几周，关注了五名受袭击影响的人的生活以及他们如何应对事后的直接后果。一位神父主持弥撒，一位寡妇为女儿洗澡，一位消防员无法停止想起坠落的躯体。这是对“数百万人中的五个人”的一个亲密观察，令人难以忘怀。

[阅读更多](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/2001-10-01/september-11th-5-people-out-of-the-multitudes/)

“世界之窗”是位于北塔顶楼的一家著名餐厅，当第一架飞机撞击大楼时，所有170名当天早上在场的员工和顾客的逃生路径都被切断。这篇文章由Cal Sussman撰写，他曾参加过品酒课程，后来成为“世界之窗”的葡萄酒司仪。这篇文章获得了詹姆斯·比尔德奖最佳个人随笔奖，探讨了幸存者的悲伤，并绘制了这家受人爱戴的纽约市机构的感人肖像。

[阅读更多](https://www.esquire.com/more/food-drink/a13524/world-trade-center-911-1102/)

Stanley Praimnath和Brian Clark分别在南塔的81层和84层工作，他们是仅有的四位来自受撞击区以上楼层的幸存者之一。Clark做出决定下楼走唯一开放的楼梯，忽略了其他人的请求去楼顶，并听到了Praimnath的求救声。两人都到达地面并逃离大楼，就在它坍塌的时候，至今他们仍是好友。

[阅读更多](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/sep/11/world-trade-center-911-survivors-stanley-praimnath-brian-clark)

这篇综合性的回顾文章结合了叙事文本、摄影、视频和数据新闻，讲述了袭击发生的第一分钟里地面上发生的事情。这17分钟指的是第一架飞机撞击北塔和第二架飞机撞击南塔之间的时间，记者Garrett M. Graff通过普通人的叙述以及军方和政府官员的叙述，展示了那一天的混乱局面。

[阅读更多](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/article/911-what-happened-the-last-17-minutes-before-the-second-plane-hit-the-twin-towers)
articles.summary:
Twenty-five years goes by in an instant. On Sept. 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked and pointed directly at the heart of the country, and life hasn’t been the same since. Though time can have a dulling effect, pushing those memories into a safe corner of one’s mind or lengthening the time between them, the awful visuals and lived experiences never go away.

It’s hard to believe, but a third of Americans were born after 9/11. But the effects of the attack—an enhanced surveillance state, increased airport security and military incursions around the world—are felt by everyone. Universal, too, are the stories of heroism, friendship and sacrifice that will forever mark that sad day.

With the 25th anniversary of 9/11 upon us, we put together a list of some of the most important journalism that took us through the day as it happened or examined it from the perspective of time. Ahead, we have 10 remarkable stories about Sept. 11, 2001. Some have been celebrated for decades; others you may never have read.

Read on to look back at the tragedy and perhaps find hope in some of the stories.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, real stories, travel, tech and trending topics all week long.

Esquire’s “The Falling Man” (2003)

On Sept. 12, 2001, the Associated Press published a photograph of an unknown man falling headfirst from the north tower of the World Trade Center. In 2003, Esquire journalist Tom Junod set out to determine who the man was by reviewing the entire series of 12 photographs taken by AP photographer Richard Drew. The result explores collective grief and trauma and has become one of the defining pieces of journalism from the post–9/11 era.

Read more at Esquire

The New York Times’s “102 Minutes” (2002)

The title of this piece refers to the amount of time that elapsed between the first plane hitting the north tower at 8:46 a.m. and its collapse at 10:28 a.m. Eight months after the attack, the New York Times published an accounting of those 102 minutes by piecing together emails and phone calls from those trapped and killed, as well as recollections from survivors. It’s as chilling now as it was when it was first published.

Read more at The New York Times

The Wall Street Journal’s breaking news reporting (2001)

The staff of the Wall Street Journal won the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting in 2002 for its 9/11 coverage. That coverage included real-time reports of the planes and collapses as well as potential impacts, including to airport security and the economy, as they were happening. One particularly harrowing story is a first-person accounting of that day called “The Eye of the Storm: One Journey Through Desperation and Chaos,” by John Bussey.

You can read all of the winning coverage at the Pulitzer Prize page, below.

Read more at The Pulitzer Prizes

The Washington Post’s “September 11, 2001” (2001)

This narrative account, published just days after 9/11, weaves together events at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and the final moments of United Flight 93, which went down in Pennsylvania. David Maraniss reconstructs the day through survivor accounts and reporting that paint a vivid picture of the chaos and destruction, as well as how it was seen through the eyes of people living through it in real time.

Read more at The Washington Post

The Atlantic’s “Twenty Years Gone” (2021)

Jennifer Senior’s devastating account of one family’s loss after the attacks won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing. Bobby McIlvaine was just 26 years old on Sept. 11, 2001, and the story of the different ways his family coped with losing their charming and ambitious son, brother and boyfriend reminds us that grief is unpredictable and personal.

Read more at The Atlantic

The New Yorker’s “The Real Heroes Are Dead” (2002)

Rick Resorla, a former British paratrooper and U.S. Army veteran, was the head of security for Morgan Stanley in the south tower of the World Trade Center. Credited with saving thousands of people, he died when he went back inside to offer more help. This piece by James B. Stewart tells the story of that day through the lens of Resorla’s personal life before the attacks, as well as through his loved ones, who subsequently had to process his heroism and death.

Read more at The New Yorker

The Washington Post’s “The Days After” (2001)

This story, published just weeks after 9/11, looks at the lives of five people who were affected by the attacks and how they dealt with the immediate aftermath. A priest delivers a mass, a widow gives her daughter a bath, a firefighter can’t stop thinking of falling bodies. It’s an intimate look at “five people out of the multitudes,” and it stays with you.

Read more at The Washington Post

Esquire’s “Drinking at 1,300 ft.: A 9/11 Story About Wine and Wisdom” (2011)

Windows on the World was a celebrated restaurant at the top of the north tower, and when the first plane hit the building, all escape routes for the 170 employees and patrons who were there that morning were severed. This story, which won a James Beard Award for Best Personal Essay, is told by Cal Sussman, a writer who took a wine class and then became a sommelier at Windows on the World. It works through survivor’s grief and paints a touching portrait of a beloved New York City institution.

Read more at Esquire

The Guardian’s “25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers …” (2026)

Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark worked on the south tower’s 81st and 84th floors, respectively, and they are two of only four known survivors of the floors above the impact zone. Clark made the fateful decision to go down the only open stairwell, ignoring pleas from others to go up to the roof, and heard Praimnath calling for help. Both reached the ground floor and ran from the building just as it collapsed, and they are still friends to this day.

Read more at The Guardian

National Geographic’s “The 17 Minutes That Changed America” (2026)

This comprehensive retrospective of the first minutes of the attack combines narrative text, photography, video and data journalism to tell the story of what was happening on the ground as the day unfolded. The 17 minutes refers to the time between the first plane hitting the north tower and the second hitting the south one, and reporter Garrett M. Graff highlights a range of accounts from regular people as well as military and government officials about the confusion of that day.

Read more at National Geographic

articles.title: You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy
articles.content:
作为一个狂热的纽约巨人队球迷（尽管最近几年战绩惨淡，但情况一定会好转！），我会无条件地观看任何一场比赛。从常规赛第一周到赛季结束，每个星期天、星期一和星期四晚上，你总能发现我守在电视机前，很可能正在对着解说员大声吼叫。

即使你对足球的认知仅限于支持的球队名称，你也一定见过聚众会议：比赛暂停后，球员们会向队友靠拢，很快就肩并肩地站成一个小圈。经过一番严肃讨论后，他们会鞠躬致敬，然后迅速奔向各自的位置。

这种场景在每一场足球比赛中都会重复出现。它如此熟悉，以至于大多数人从未停下来思考过它的由来。为什么足球运动员要聚众会议呢？

原来，这种足球特色行为有着鲜明的起源，而且你很可能猜不到。为了了解足球中最具代表性的仪式之一，我采访了两位专家：足球历史学家肯·克里彭（Ken Crippen），也是足球学习学院的创始人，以及职业足球名人堂档案与展馆副总裁乔恩·肯德尔（Jon Kendle）。

无论你是懂得“闪电突袭”和“镍币配置”之分，还是仅仅喜欢观看比赛（或是零食），我们保证你会发现这篇文章非常有趣。继续阅读，在开球之前找到答案。

《读者文摘》的“阅读提升”新闻通讯提供更多有趣的事实、娱乐、幽默、旅行和科技内容。

美国足球的根源可以追溯到足球和橄榄球，1869年罗格斯大学和普林斯顿大学之间的第一场大学足球比赛标志着其开始。1880年代，耶鲁大学球员兼教练沃尔特·坎普（Walter Camp），被称为“美国足球之父”，制定了与橄榄球日益分离的规则。

当时的比赛与今日大相径庭。克里彭指出：“足球刚刚出现时，前传是非法的。你会看到大规模的冲击性动作和大量的体能对抗。”

这种体能对抗甚至可能致命。他补充道：“球场上有太多球员死去，以至于报纸会进行连续报道。”足球仍然在探索自身，从比赛方式到球队的比赛中沟通方式。

早期足球中，四分卫简单地召唤或示意比赛——通常就在攻防线上。当然，“这存在问题，因为防守方可以听到比赛指令”，克里彭指出。

另一种选择是在球队接近攻防线时召唤比赛，“但距离足够远，以至于防守方无法听到”，他说道。

这造成了明显的战略问题：如果防守方能听到比赛指令，他们可以相应调整。球队需要一种在不暴露计划的情况下沟通的方式。

足球聚众会议广泛归功于加洛德大学，现在的加洛德大学，是华盛顿特区一所为聋哑学生服务的学校。加洛德大学的足球队由聋哑球员组成，他们通过手语交流，在场上面临独特的挑战。

根据肯德尔的说法，由于对手通常是为听障学生服务的学校，加洛德大学四分卫保罗·哈伯德（Paul Hubbard）担心他们在观察他的手势以读懂球队意图。哈伯德的解决方案是形成一个圆圈，这样对手就无法读懂他的手势。

这个圆圈成为了第一个足球聚众会议。虽然无法确定首次亮相的具体比赛，但克里彭表示，这种做法似乎在1894年加洛德大学主要与宾夕法尼亚聋哑学校和纽约聋哑学校比赛的赛季中自然产生。

肯德尔将聚众会议称为“一个充满魔力和特殊信任的地方”，但它并未立即成为足球的普遍组成部分。

阿莫斯·阿隆佐·斯塔格（Amos Alonzo Stagg），作为该运动的早期重要创新者之一，1896年在芝加哥大学执教时开始使用聚众会议。但足球界花了很长时间才跟上这一流行趋势。克里彭说：“斯塔格是一个创新者，无论他做什么，其他大学球队通常都会效仿。”然而，聚众会议“直到20世纪20年代才真正流行起来。”

但聚众会议的有用性也创造了新的问题：球队可以用它来浪费时间。克里彭说：“一些人认为这是一种有意的拖延战术。”这导致30年代制定了规则，限制球队在聚众会议中花费过多时间。最终，1976年引入的比赛计时器使这些限制不再必要。如今，NFL给进攻方设定了开始下一场比赛的固定时间。

有趣的是：没有规则规定足球队必须聚众会议。根据当前的NFL规则，“聚众会议是指两名或两名以上球员在比赛场地或终场区中，与其位于正常发球、自由球或公平接球踢球位置，形成一个小组，以接收下一场比赛的指令或任何其他原因。”

聚众会议内部发生了什么，由进攻方决定。在典型的聚众会议中，四分卫传达下一场比赛的指令。肯德尔指出，这可以“涉及阵型、动作、发球计数、阻截方案、外接手路线以及跑卫应该通过哪个缺口”。

聚众会议也给进攻方一个机会暂时停止。克里彭说：“这使球队可以看到谁受伤、疲劳，或是注意到进攻方可以利用的防守漏洞。”

肯德尔补充道，聚众会议可以隐藏进攻方的阵型，使防守方在发球前更难正确布防。

因为有时候战胜防守的最佳方式就是拒绝给他们反应时间。于是，无聚众会议进攻应运而生：与其聚集讨论下一场比赛，进攻方立即布阵。NFL将其描述为一种可以节省时间、出其不意以及阻止防守方换人替补的策略。

根据肯德尔的说法，1980年代和1990年代初，辛辛那提孟加拉虎队和水牛城公牛队采用了“无聚众会议”进攻。公牛队及其“快速进攻”进攻连续四次杀入超级碗。

顺便一提：无聚众会议足球并非新鲜事。克里彭追溯其使用历史至约翰·海斯曼（John Heisman），是的，奖杯以他命名，他在1899年奥本大学采用这种进攻方式。

如果聚众会议最初是为了简化和保密交流而发明的，现代技术已经使比赛指令传递更加容易。

1940年代，克利夫兰棕榈队教练保罗·布朗（Paul Brown）使用“传令后卫”系统，其中替补球员可以带着来自场边的比赛进入比赛。布朗还在1950年代实验过无线电头盔，尽管直到1994年NFL才开始使用无线电头盔，允许场边与场上四分卫之间的有限交流，根据肯德尔的说法。

技术继续推动足球交流的发展。2023年，加洛德大学和AT&T推出了一个5G连接的足球头盔，允许教练在平板电脑上选择比赛并将其发送到四分卫头盔内的数字显示屏。

可能不会——至少不完全如此。

“我认为聚众会议仍然是足球的重要组成部分”，肯德尔说。“它使球队可以团结在一起，接收关键指令，确保所有人都在同一页面上。”

所以下次你看到足球比赛中进攻方围绕四分卫聚集时，花点时间感受一下你所看到的。聚众会议可能看起来只是比赛之间的一个简单暂停，但它是足球中最持久的战略工具之一——给予球员一个交流、重组并思考接下来步骤的时刻。

现在，如果不介意的话，我要去看足球比赛了。

这篇文章《你永远猜不到足球聚众会议的起源——这个策略背后的迷人历史》最初发表在《读者文摘》。
articles.summary:
I firmly believe that the only good thing about the end of summer is the beginning of football season. Though I’m a die-hard New York Giants fan (it’s been a rough few years, but things are gonna turn around!), I’ll watch any and every game I can. On Sundays—and Monday and Thursday nights—from Week 1 through the postseason, you’ll find me near a TV, very likely yelling at the announcers.

But even if the extent of your football knowledge is the name of the team your family roots for, you’ve seen the huddle: The action ends, the players wander back toward one another, and suddenly they’re standing shoulder to shoulder in a little circle. There’s some serious discussion, a few nods, and then they break apart and race to their positions.

It happens over and over, in every football game. It’s such a familiar part of the sport that most of us never stop to wonder about it. But why do football players huddle?

As it turns out, this football staple has a very distinct origin—and it’s one you’d likely never guess. For the deets on one of football’s most recognizable rituals, I turned to two experts: football historian Ken Crippen, founder of the Football Learning Academy, and Jon Kendle, vice president of Archives and Exhibits at the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Whether you know a blitz from a nickel package or just enjoy the game (or the snacks), we guarantee that you’ll find this fascinating. Read on for the answer before kickoff.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, humor, travel and tech.

How did football get its start?

The roots of American football trace back to both soccer and rugby, with the first college football game between Rutgers and Princeton in 1869. In the 1880s, Yale player and coach Walter Camp, who became known as the “father of American football,” helped establish rules that increasingly separated American football from rugby.

The game was barely recognizable by today’s standards. “When it first emerged, forward passing was illegal,” says Crippen. “You would see mass-momentum plays and a lot of physicality.”

And that physicality could be deadly. “So many players died on the field that they would have running counts in the newspapers,” he adds. Football was a game still figuring itself out, from how it was played to how teams communicated in the middle of it.

How did players communicate before the huddle?

In the early days of football, quarterbacks simply called or signaled the play—often right at the line of scrimmage. Of course, this “was a problem because the defense could hear the play call,” Crippen notes.

Another option was to call the play while the team was approaching the line of scrimmage, “but far enough away that the defense could not hear them,” he says.

That created an obvious strategic problem: If the defense could hear the play call, it could adjust accordingly. Teams needed a way to communicate without giving away their plans.

How did the huddle get its start?

The football huddle is widely credited to Gallaudet College, now Gallaudet University, a school for deaf students in Washington, D.C. Gallaudet’s football team was made up of deaf players who communicated using sign language, creating a unique challenge on the field.

Because their opponents were often schools for the hearing-impaired, Gallaudet quarterback Paul Hubbard worried they were watching his hands to read his team’s intentions, according to Kendle. Hubbard’s solution was to form a circle so opponents couldn’t read his signs.

That circle became the first football huddle. The exact game in which it debuted is unknown, but Crippen says the practice appears to have developed organically during Gallaudet’s 1894 season, when the team primarily played the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf and the New York School for the Deaf.

When did the huddle become widespread, and why?

The huddle—which Kendle calls “a magical and special place of trust”—didn’t immediately become a universal part of football.

Amos Alonzo Stagg, one of the sport’s great early innovators, began using the huddle while coaching at the University of Chicago in 1896. But it took a while for the rest of football to catch on. “Stagg was an innovator, and whatever he did was usually copied by other college teams,” Crippen says. Still, the huddle “did not really catch on until the 1920s.”

But the huddle’s usefulness created a new problem: Teams could use it to waste time. “Some saw it as an intentional stall tactic,” Crippen says. That led to rules in the 1930s designed to keep teams from spending too much time in the huddle. Eventually, the introduction of the play clock in 1976 made those restrictions unnecessary. Today, the NFL gives offenses a set amount of time to begin the next play. 

What are the rules of the huddle?

Here’s the funny thing: There’s no rule saying a football team needs to huddle. According to the current NFL Rulebook, “a huddle is the action of two or more players in the field of play or in the end zone who, instead of assuming their normal position for the snap, free kick or fair catch kick, form a group for receiving instructions for the next play or for any other reason.”

What happens inside that circle is up to the offense. In a typical huddle, the quarterback communicates instructions for the next play. That, notes Kendle, can “be for the formation, motions, snap count, blocking schemes, wide receiver routes and which gap the running back should run through.”

The huddle also gives the offense a moment to take stock. “It allows the team to see who is hurt, tired or seeing something that the offense can take advantage of against the defense,” Crippen says.

Kendle adds that the huddle can conceal the offense’s formation, making it more difficult for the defense to line up correctly before the snap.

Why doesn’t the offense huddle before every play?

Because sometimes the best way to beat a defense is to deny it time to respond. Enter the no-huddle offense: Rather than gathering to discuss the next play, the offense lines up immediately. The NFL describes it as a strategy that can conserve time, catch the defense off guard and prevent defensive substitutions.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Cincinnati Bengals and Buffalo Bills featured “no-huddle” offenses, according to Kendle. The Bills and their “hurry-up” offense advanced to four consecutive Super Bowls.

By the way: No-huddle football is hardly new. Crippen traces its use back to John Heisman (yes, the trophy is named for him), who used the offense at Auburn in 1899.

How is technology changing this football staple?

If the huddle was invented to make communication easier and more secretive, modern technology has made communicating plays much easier.

In the 1940s, Cleveland Browns coach Paul Brown used a “messenger guard” system, in which a substitute player could enter the game with the play from the sideline. Brown also experimented with radio headsets in the 1950s, though it wasn’t until 1994 that the NFL instituted radio helmets to allow limited communication from the sidelines to the quarterback on the field, according to Kendle.

Technology has continued to advance football communication. In 2023, Gallaudet University and AT&T debuted a 5G-connected football helmet that allowed a coach to select a play on a tablet and send it to a digital display inside the quarterback’s helmet.

Will the football huddle ever disappear?

Probably not—or, at least, not entirely.

“I believe the huddle is still an essential part of football,” Kendle says. “It allows the team to come together as a unit to receive critical instructions and make sure they are on the same page.”

So the next time you watch a football game and see the offense gather around their quarterback, take a second to appreciate what you’re actually looking at. The huddle may look like a simple pause between plays, but it’s one of football’s most enduring strategic tools—giving players a moment to communicate, regroup and figure out what comes next.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a football game to watch.

  • Jon Kendle, vice president of Archives and Exhibits at the Pro Football Hall of Fame; email interview, Sept. 8, 2026
